title: The Debt Didn’t Move
narrativeQuestion: What happens when the price of what you sell falls while the number you owe refuses to change?

chapters.title: The Number That Didn’t Move
chapters.claim: Falling crop prices made a fixed nominal debt harder to repay in real terms.

chapters.title: More
chapters.claim: Greater agricultural productivity could coexist with falling unit prices and financial pressure.

chapters.title: One Way Out
chapters.claim: Railroads connected farmers to national markets while creating dependence on a narrow transportation chokepoint.

chapters.title: Two True Things
chapters.claim: Higher western freight rates and lower western traffic density were both real, making the rate dispute an economic conflict rather than a cartoon.

chapters.title: They Tried Regulation First
chapters.claim: Interstate commerce outgrew state regulation and helped drive the creation of federal railroad regulation in 1887.

chapters.title: First, Help Each Other
chapters.claim: Farm organizations first tried cooperation, information sharing, and collective buying and selling before turning fully to party politics.

chapters.title: The Other Alliance
chapters.claim: Black farmers built the Colored Farmers’ Alliance because white southern Alliances excluded them, showing both agrarian agency and the limits of interracial coalition.

chapters.title: Wall Street
chapters.claim: Mary Elizabeth Lease gave farmers a systemic explanation connecting local debt and rail problems to concentrated national finance.

chapters.title: Omaha
chapters.claim: The 1892 Omaha Platform assembled separate grievances into a coherent national political program.

chapters.title: Sixteen to One
chapters.claim: Free silver appealed differently to debtors, creditors, and wage earners because inflation changes real burdens and purchasing power unevenly.

chapters.title: Twenty-Two
chapters.claim: James B. Weaver’s 1892 campaign won 22 electoral votes and made the People’s Party a visible national third force.

chapters.title: The Deal
chapters.claim: Populist fusion behind Democrat William Jennings Bryan in 1896 traded independent party identity for a larger free-silver coalition.

chapters.title: November 3
chapters.claim: Bryan’s defeat in 1896 ended the campaign’s immediate path to power without erasing the ideas Populists had pushed into national politics.

chapters.title: Some Numbers Moved
chapters.claim: Some Populist demands later entered mainstream law while other major demands did not.

chapters.title: The Words Make More Sense Now
chapters.claim: Vocabulary becomes meaningful after the economic relationships have been made visible.

chapters.title: Before You Leave, Fix the Story
chapters.claim: Note repair preserves the complicated version: monetary pressure, two-sided rail economics, Black agrarian organization, and a mixed legacy.

accuracyNotes: The $500 debt is illustrative and must never be presented as an average farm mortgage.
Do not reduce the farm crisis to overproduction alone; productivity, world markets, credit, monetary conditions, transportation, tariffs, weather, and depression all mattered.
Western freight rates were higher, while western rail traffic density was also lower; preserve both sides of the rate conflict.
The ICC was historically significant, but its early enforcement power was limited.
Free silver was expected by supporters to expand money and ease debtor pressure; do not present it as a guaranteed cure.
Do not use ‘raise less corn and more hell’ as a verified Mary Elizabeth Lease quotation.
Black farmers were political organizers with their own institutions; white southern Alliances excluded them and interracial cooperation had serious limits.
Bryan remained a Democrat in 1896; Populists endorsed him through fusion.
Later reforms echo Populist demands but were not single-handedly caused by the Populist Party.
